title: Verbs Followed by Gerund Only — 50 Must-Know Expressions for SSC CGL
excerpt: Master the 50 verbs that take only gerunds. Complete exam-focused list, common traps, step-by-step strategy and practice questions for SSC CGL, Bank PO and Railway aspirants.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
In every SSC CGL, Bank PO and Railway paper, 1–2 marks are quietly lost on Error Spotting or Sentence Improvement because students confuse gerund-only verbs with infinitive verbs. Textbooks give long lists but never show how these 50 expressions actually appear in the mixed-pattern sentences examiners love. After 22 years in the classroom I can tell you: the marks slip away not because the list is difficult, but because students treat each verb as an isolated fact instead of one connected system.

Quick Answer: Certain verbs in English are followed only by a gerund (V-ing) and never by an infinitive (to + V1). Memorise the closed family of 50 must-know expressions below and you will never again accept “enjoy to swim” or “suggest to go” as correct in the exam.

Why Verbs Followed by Gerund Only Feel Harder Than They Are

Students enter class thinking “gerund means any -ing form”. That half-understanding is exactly what the examiner exploits. The real test is whether you can instantly recognise the verb that forces the gerund and reject the attractive “to + verb” option that sounds natural to the Indian ear.

  • The list looks endless, so most students memorise 10–12 verbs and hope the rest will not appear.
  • Many verbs can take both gerund and infinitive; students freely transfer that freedom to pure-gerund verbs.
  • Error Spotting sentences hide the key verb inside a relative clause or after a long subject.
  • Cloze tests offer four options that all “sound correct” until the fixed pattern is applied.
  • Textbooks never show the same verb in affirmative, negative and question forms the way the actual paper does.

In my classroom I have watched otherwise strong students lose 3–4 marks in every mock simply because they treated “enjoy”, “avoid” and “suggest” as separate facts instead of one closed family that always demands the -ing form.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Using the infinitive after pure-gerund verbs
The most expensive habit. Students write “I enjoy to read” or “She suggested to postpone” because the infinitive feels more formal or “exam-like”. In the paper this is an automatic error.

2. Mixing “both-possible” verbs with “gerund-only” verbs
Begin, start, continue, like, love can take either form. Students apply the same liberty to admit, deny, mind, finish and risk – and the mark disappears.

3. Ignoring the object + gerund pattern
After appreciate, mind, imagine, prevent the structure is often verb + object + gerund. Students either drop the object or insert “to” instead of -ing.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Infinitive after pure-gerund verb

Students prefer “to + V1” because it feels formal.

Wrong: He enjoys to swim in the morning.

Correct: He enjoys swimming in the morning.

❌
Mistake 2: Treating “suggest / recommend” like “advise”

Advise can take infinitive; suggest and recommend cannot.

Wrong: She suggested to postpone the meeting.

Correct: She suggested postponing the meeting.

❌
Mistake 3: Missing the object + gerund structure

After mind / appreciate the object is required before the gerund.

Wrong: Would you mind to open the window?

Correct: Would you mind opening the window?

The Complete Gerund-Only Verb System, Step by Step

Treat the following 50 verbs as one closed family. The moment any of them appears, the next verb must be in the -ing form. No exceptions in the exam.

Step 1 – Memorise the pure-gerund family as one unit
Write all 50 verbs on a single page. Read them aloud every morning for seven days. The moment you see any of these verbs, your brain must automatically expect -ing.

❌ She avoids to speak to him.
✅ She avoids speaking to him. (Avoid belongs to the gerund-only family)

Step 2 – Spot the verb first in Error Spotting
Ignore the rest of the sentence. Locate the main verb. If it is from the list, the following verb must be -ing.

Step 3 – Watch for the object + gerund pattern
Appreciate, mind, imagine and prevent frequently take an object before the gerund.

❌ I appreciate to help me.
✅ I appreciate your helping me. (Object + gerund)

Step 4 – Eliminate the attractive infinitive at once
In four-option questions the infinitive almost always looks more “correct”. Cross it out the moment the verb is identified as gerund-only.

Step 5 – Practise mixed-pattern sentences
Examiners love to place two gerund-only verbs in one sentence or combine them with prepositions.

Step 6 – Create ten original sentences daily
Write one affirmative, one negative and one question for each new verb. Recognition turns into automatic response.

Signal Group What it tells you in the exam
admit, deny, confessNext verb must be gerund
enjoy, dislike, detest, can’t standFeeling verbs → gerund only
finish, complete, quit, give upCompletion verbs → gerund only
suggest, recommend, considerSuggestion verbs → gerund only
mind, appreciate + objectObject + gerund pattern
avoid, risk, escape, evadeAvoidance verbs → gerund only

Step-by-Step Strategy

1 Identify the verb that can take a second verb.

2 Check whether it belongs to the 50-gerund-only list.

3 If yes, reject every “to + V1” option immediately.

4 Confirm the -ing form is present and grammatically correct.

5 Watch for object + gerund or preposition + gerund.

6 Mark the answer and move on – never second-guess a pure-gerund verb.

A Quick Turnaround Story

Last monsoon a Bank PO aspirant in my batch was stuck at 23–24 in English mocks. His Error Spotting accuracy on gerund-infinitive items was below 40 %. We spent one focused class only on the 50 gerund-only verbs. He wrote each verb with three original sentences. In the next mock the sentence “The manager suggested to postpone the interview” appeared. He crossed “to postpone” in under four seconds and scored 31. The difference was not new knowledge – it was recognition speed created by treating the verbs as one system.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • One-page wall chart – Write the 50 verbs on a single sheet and stick it above your study table. Look at it every time you sit down.
  • Never learn a verb alone – Always pair it with its fixed pattern: “enjoy + V-ing”, “suggest + V-ing”.
  • Cloze-test first scan – The moment you see any of these 50 verbs, the blank after it is almost certainly a gerund.
  • Previous-year practice only after mastery – Doing PYQs before internalising the list only reinforces the wrong “feel”.
  • Teach one verb daily – Explaining the pattern to a friend locks it permanently in memory.

The Bottom Line

Verbs followed by gerund only are not fifty separate rules. They are one closed family. Once you treat them as a single system, Error Spotting and Sentence Improvement questions on this topic become almost mechanical. Master the list, apply the six-step strategy, and these marks will stop slipping away.

Practice Questions

Q1 (SSC CGL Exam Pattern): The committee suggested to postpone the meeting until next month.

**Summary:** Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: suggested postponing / suggested that the meeting be postponed

Explanation: “Suggest” belongs to the pure-gerund family. After suggest we use V-ing (or a that-clause). “To postpone” is incorrect in standard exam English.

Q2 (Bank PO Exam Pattern): Would you mind to open the window? It is very hot in here.

**Summary:** Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: Would you mind opening the window?

Explanation: “Mind” is always followed by a gerund. The structure is mind + V-ing. “To open” is a classic trap.

Q3 (Railway / SSC Pattern): He avoided to speak to the media after the incident.

**Summary:** Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: He avoided speaking to the media after the incident.

Explanation: “Avoid” is a pure-gerund verb. It can never be followed by an infinitive in the language of competitive exams.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. Are there really only 50 verbs that take gerund only?
For SSC CGL, Bank PO and Railway exams the 50 listed above cover virtually every question that appears. Rare or advanced verbs are almost never tested.
Q2. Can “suggest” ever take an infinitive?
No. In formal and exam English “suggest” is followed by a gerund or a that-clause. “Suggest to do” is always marked wrong.
Q3. What about like, love, hate, begin and start?
These verbs can take both gerund and infinitive with little or no change in meaning. They do not belong to the gerund-only list.
Q4. How many questions on this topic usually appear in SSC CGL Tier-1?
Usually 1–2 questions in Error Spotting or Sentence Improvement. One correct answer can decide the final rank.
Q5. Is “look forward to” followed by gerund?
Yes. Here “to” is a preposition, so the correct form is look forward to + gerund (look forward to meeting you). This is a related but separate pattern.
